newsitem.title: UK: Full text of December 11 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of December 11 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the December 11 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on 11 December, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments

2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by officials before the meeting) provided further evidence that cost pressures remained moderate. However, there were continuing signs that output growth was picking up, and recent indicators of business confidence and consumer demand remained strong.
Inflation Indicators

3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest payments - RPIX) rose by 0.4 percentage points in October, to 3.3 per cent, due partly to the fall in the price level in October 1995 dropping out of the year-on-year inflation figures. All-items RPI inflation rose by 0.6 percentage points, to 2.7 per cent.
4. Most other price and cost indicators confirmed that inflationary pressures remained moderate:
- sterling non-oil commodity prices fell by 0.3 per cent in October. However, the oil price had risen again slightly to $23.7 per barrel;
- sterling's effective exchange rate index had continued to rise sharply from 89.3 before the last meeting to 93.1 currently;

- total non-oil import prices fell by 1.4 per cent in the three months to September compared to the previous three months, and were 2.1 per cent lower than a year ago. Non-EU import prices fell by 0.9 per cent in the three months to October on the previous three months;

- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) fell in November by 2.3 per cent; and compared to a year ago they were 7.2 per cent lower. The CIPS survey input price indicator also fell in November;

- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) rose by 0.1 per cent in November; but the annual inflation rate fell to 0.8 per cent, from 0.9 per cent in October. The CBI survey output price expectations balance fell slightly in November;
- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings was unchanged in September, at 4 per cent; and IRS median pay settlements were also unchanged at 3.0 per cent in September.
Monetary and Financial Indicators
5. Notes and coin grew by 0.7 per cent in November, up from 0.4 per cent in October; and the annual growth rate rose slightly, to 7.4 per cent. M0's annual growth rate was unchanged at 7.4 per cent.
6. M4 grew by 1.1 per cent in October, up from 0.8 per cent in September. The annual growth rate of M4 and M4 lending rose, to 10.3 per cent, and 9.5 per cent, respectively.

7. The Halifax house price index rose by 0.5 per cent in November, and it was up 7.2 per cent on a year earlier. The Nationwide index rose by 1.3 per cent in November, 8.8 per cent up on a year earlier. Housing market transactions continued to grow strongly; in the three months to October particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) were 8.4 per cent up on the previous three months, and 18.9 per cent up on a year earlier.

8. Short-term interest rates were little changed in the US and Japan since the last meeting, but had risen by nearly 10 basis points in Germany. Following the rise in base rates, UK short-term interest rates had risen by almost 35 basis points; and forward rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts had also risen (by up to 35 basis points) at all maturities.

9. 10-year bond yields had fallen by over 20 basis points in the US and Germany, and by around 10 basis points in Japan. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had risen for shorter maturities, but had fallen by over 25 basis points for 20-year maturities. Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) had fallen by around 10 basis points and 40 basis points for 5 and 10 years ahead respectively.
Activity Indicators

10. In the US recent data confirmed that output growth was slowing to a more sustainable rate. The preliminary estimate of US GDP growth in Q3 was 0.5 per cent, leaving it 2.0 per cent up on a year earlier. Industrial production fell by 0.5 per cent in October, following a rise of 0.3 per cent in September. In Japan the preliminary estimate of Q3 GDP growth was 0.1 per cent, leaving it 3.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Industrial production rose by 3.5 per cent in October, following a rise of 1.5 per cent in September.

11. In Germany the preliminary estimate of Q3 GDP growth was stronger than expected at 0.8 per cent, leaving it 1.9 per cent up on a year earlier. But industrial production fell by 1.8 per cent in October, following a fall of 0.6 per cent in September. In France growth rebounded as expected, with GDP rising by 0.9 per cent in Q3.

12. The latest estimates of UK GDP growth in Q3 showed that both whole economy and non-oil GDP grew by 0.8 per cent, and were respectively 2.4 per cent and 2.3 per cent higher than a year earlier. Consumer spending rose by 1.1 per cent in Q3, leaving it 3.3 per cent up on a year earlier. Investment fell by 2.2 per cent in Q3, but it was 3.1 per cent higher than a year earlier.
13. Most other activity data were consistent with a continuing pick-up in growth, and indicators of business confidence and consumer demand remained strong:

- manufacturing output rose by 0.5 per cent in October, but in the three months to October it was up just 0.1 per cent on a year earlier. Total industrial output fell by 0.1 per cent in October, but in the latest three months was up 0.7 per cent on a year earlier;
- all major business surveys were more buoyant. The November CIPS and CBI surveys both showed an increase in new orders indicators. The November CBI Regional Trends Survey was also stronger;

- retail sales rose by 0.4 per cent in October, following a fall of 0.3 per cent in September; and in the three months to October sales were 4.0 per cent higher than in the same period a year earlier;

- survey indicators in the retail sector also remained strong: consumer confidence rose to its highest level since August 1988, and the November CBI Distributive Trades Survey showed a rise in the balance of retailers expecting higher sales;
- claimant unemployment fell by 40,800 in October, and unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres rose by 9,300.
Summary of discussion

14. The Governor said that since the last meeting six weeks ago the new data had broadly confirmed the underlying picture of consumer-led expansion that was discussed then. Meanwhile the exchange rate had strengthened significantly further, which had helped to hold down producer price inflation; but retail price inflation (RPIX) had remained uncomfortably strong.

15. Monetary growth had continued at rates which were unlikely to be consistent with 2-1/2 per cent RPIX inflation into the medium-term. Notes and coin had risen by 0.4 per cent in October (as in September) but substantially faster in November (+0.7 per cent) to leave the 12-month rate above 7 per cent. Broad money had increased sharply in October (by 1.1 per cent) partly as a result of gilt repo business; adjusting for that the 12-month rate remained somewhat above 9 per cent. The 12-month rate for retail M4 had picked up slightly to just over 5 per cent. M4 lending had also risen sharply in October (+0.9 per cent) to give a 12-month increase (adjusted for repo) of 8 per cent - a little above the September figure.

16. The Governor noted that total output growth was still estimated to have risen by 0.8 per cent in Q3 - an annualised average rate of 2.4 per cent over the year so far. The service sector had remained buoyant (+0.9 per cent) and manufacturing output was now reported to have risen by 0.6 per cent in Q3 and by a further 0.5 per cent in October. The survey evidence reported that orders were at their highest level for a year. Construction output had risen modestly in Q3 and that was expected to continue in Q4.

17. But there had been some puzzling expenditure estimates, including revisions, with total final domestic demand growth put at an annualised rate of 3 per cent (Q3 1996 on Q4 1995) and apparently moderating during the course of the year. Investment in particular had been revised down and had been particularly weak in Q3. These data were, however, inconsistent with most of the other indicators, and they included both a large "alignment adjustment" and "statistical discrepancy" so that the Bank was disinclined to take them at face value. As it was they showed consumption growth at an annual rate of almost 4 per cent (and over 4 per cent annualised in Q3 itself) which was comfortably above trend. This seemed likely to continue in Q4, with retail sales volumes having risen by 0.9 per cent in the 3 months to October - and a high proportion of retailers expecting strong growth in November and December (although the latest figures from the British Retail Consortium were slightly weaker for November). The housing market had remained quite strong with prices now up by 7.2 per cent on a year ago (on the Halifax index) and rising levels of transactions.

18. Reflecting the growth in output, unemployment had continued to fall, by around 40,000 in both September and October - double the average for the past year. Even so the underlying increase in average earnings had remained at 4 per cent in September (as it had since July) and pay settlements at around 3-1/2 per cent.

19. The Governor said that, as noted at the last meeting, the upswing had not up to that point been accompanied by significant inflationary cost or price pressures. And the combination of a fall in the dollar oil price (-5 per cent on average in November against October) and the further strengthening of sterling (up 3.3 per cent on the ERI since the closing rate on the day of the last meeting, and nearly 11 per cent up from the trough in early August) brought a sharp fall in producer input prices last month (a fall of 3.2 per cent in the month, for a 5 per cent annual fall; and ex FBTP down 2.3 per cent in the month, and 7 per cent on a year ago). Output price inflation, too, remained low, at +0.8 per cent on a year ago for November (ex FBTP).

20. Retail price inflation on the other hand remained disappointingly high. RPIX inflation had risen from 2.9 per cent in the year to September to 3.3 per cent in October. Prices within the services sector appeared to be rising across a broad front, reflecting the continuing growth of demand and activity. Goods prices (apart from petrol) remained generally subdued, reflecting the low rate of output price inflation, although rising prices for footwear and clothing for example might well reflect stronger demand.

21. The Governor said that, pulling all this together, the Bank would expect RPIX inflation to remain above 3 per cent into early next year and then to fall gently towards the 2-1/2 per cent target helped by the effect of the stronger exchange rate on import prices. But the Bank still expected that it would begin to pick up again later in 1997 and into 1998 as the upswing in domestic demand and in output gathered pace. On a two-year view the Bank still thought that the odds were that inflation would be above 2-1/2 per cent - and with the risks on the upside.

22. In order to moderate the upswing in domestic demand and so to stand a realistic chance of achieving the inflation target over this time horizon, the Bank was fairly confident on the basis of the present evidence that interest rates would need to rise, certainly by 1/2 per cent, in the next few months. To keep ahead of the game the Bank would advise an immediate 1/4 per cent move this month. Although the Bank could not claim that it was crucial to move again now, if rates were not raised this month, it was quite likely on the information that was already available that the Bank would need to advise a 1/2 per cent move in either January or February.

23. The Chancellor agreed on the need to stay ahead of the game in setting monetary policy. Hitting the inflation target was the best way to ensure that the healthy recovery would continue. He said the difference between himself and the Governor was on the pace of policy tightening. Interest rates had been raised at the last meeting and he was not persuaded that data published during the past month justified another increase in interest rates now. The data showed healthy growth in the economy, but this was in line with expectations and the pace was not speeding up.

24. The Chancellor noted that sterling had risen by over 4 per cent since before the last meeting. This was partly an over-reaction to last month's interest rate rise which the markets had interpreted as the beginning of a period of interest rate rises.

25. The activity data were very much in line with expectations. Retail sales had risen by 1/2 per cent in October and were 4 per cent up on a year earlier. These were encouraging figures but not dramatic. The Chancellor noted that early indications from the British Retail Consortium suggested that there had been a slowdown in sales in November compared with October. Car registrations had also fallen back a little.

26. The news on manufacturing was encouraging, pointing to a more balanced recovery. Manufacturing output had risen by 1/2 per cent in October, but comparing the last 3 months manufacturing output was still only 0.1 per cent up on a year earlier. It was not surprising, at this stage of the recovery, that business investment was beginning to strengthen. In fact, it was rather surprising that it had not strengthened more.

27. The Chancellor said that underlying RPI inflation had risen over the last month to over 3 per cent. He expected it to stay close to that rate for some months, given the profile of the index a year before. But this underlined the fact that the retail prices index was essentially a backward looking indicator. Whether inflation fell back to 2-1/2 per cent in the first part of next year depended on policy decisions taken 12-18 months before.

28. The Chancellor said that producer price inflation continued to fall. Aggregate output prices rose by 2.1 per cent in the year to November, down from 2.3 per cent in October. Excluding FBTP producer output prices rose by 0.8 per cent in the year to November, compared to 0.9 per cent in October: the best performance in almost 30 years. Producer input prices were still falling. Commodity prices were still very weak and oil prices, which had been rising sharply, had fallen back over the last month. Given the strength of the exchange rate and weak commodity prices, low producer price inflation was not surprising; and the exchange rate could be expected to reduce these pressures further.

29. Whole economy earnings growth was unchanged in September and manufacturing pay settlements remained flat at around 3-1/4 per cent. Unemployment had fallen more rapidly in recent months but the Chancellor felt that the level of unemployment had further to fall before it had any significant effect on inflationary pressures.

30. The Chancellor said that the housing market was improving. Building societies' house price inflation figures were between 7 and 9 per cent, but these increases were still concentrated in certain regions. Although previous housing market recoveries had started in London, there were many differences between the current situation and the housing market in the late 1980s. The level of house prices in relation to earnings was well below that in the late 1980s, as was the rate of house price inflation.

31. Money growth had picked up a little. The annual growth of M0 was 7.4 per cent in November, compared to 7.3 per cent in October. M4 growth had picked up also, but it still remained around 10 per cent, as it had been for the last year. While these signs should not be ignored, it was not clear in current circumstances that they had inflationary implications.

32. Overall, the Chancellor thought the picture was still mixed, with the indicators giving differing signals. While many of the indicators pointed to accelerating activity, there were some notable exceptions, in particular, the early indication of a slowdown in retail sales for November, the fall in car registrations and the continuing fall in producer prices. He thought the case had not been made for a further rise in interest rates this month.
33. In discussion the following points were made:

- the pick-up in growth was being led by consumer demand. There were signs that retail activity growth may have slowed somewhat in November; but retail statistics were particularly volatile around the Christmas period, and subject to distortion. With the saving ratio still high, disposable income rising quickly and a number of building society windfalls in the offing, the conditions remained in place for continuing rapid growth in consumption;

- another factor underpinning the consumer pick-up was likely to be the recovery in the housing market, which was now well-established. As in previous recoveries, prices were rising fastest in London and the South East. However, prices were still low in relation to earnings, and housing turnover was still at an historically low level;

- although manufacturing output was rising, the recovery in this sector was still relatively muted, and investment was not growing as rapidly as had been expected. Also the indirect tax increases introduced in the Budget had already been implemented and would have an immediate impact on demand;

- the recent rise in the exchange rate appeared to be exerting some downward pressure on producer prices, which were very subdued. Strong international competition would also continue to limit inflationary pressures in the tradeables sector. However, parts of the economy (in particular in services) were less exposed to these competitive pressures. And both earnings and price inflation had risen more quickly in the service sector;

- the very moderate cost pressures in the economy had not been fully reflected in retail price inflation (which remained above the 2-1/2 per cent target). The rise in service price inflation appeared to be in response to strong demand in that sector. But goods prices at the retail level were also relatively strong, suggesting that consumers may be starting to show less resistance to price increases.
Conclusion

34. Summing up, the Chancellor said that the objective shared by all was to set interest rates at the level necessary to hit the inflation target. This meant raising interest rates at the first sign of inflationary pressures, as he had done last month. Although activity continued to pick up, this was in line with expectations; and he felt the evidence over the last month did not justify a further rise in interest rates. He decided therefore to leave interest rates unchanged for the moment.
H M Treasury
